56	
57	Each: one sentence, an everyday example, and the past decision it seems to go against, in the owner's words.
58	
59	**C1.** *In one sentence:* each part of an explanation has to match what its piece of the thing does inside the whole, not the rule that piece follows on its own. *Example:* a bicycle's gear part may only say "the wheel turns at the speed it turns now with this rider", not "the gears multiply whatever the pedals do". On your shop sign, the red-part and blue-part explanation would no longer be an explanation, however the change of day is read. *Seems to go against* S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."
60	
61	**C2.** *In one sentence:* only a question that was itself found or worked out can be answered; a question simply laid down has no answer. *Example:* a customer just asks "why is the sign red on Mondays?", with no story of how the question arose; on the reading that such a question counts as laid down, nothing explains the sign, the weathervane, or what your engineer's bridge creates. Where the question's story is recorded as found or worked out, nothing changes. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."; S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained"; S41 Q6: "Yes, it can".
62	
63	**C5.** *In one sentence:* a difference counts towards an explanation only when it comes with a change made to the thing, not from its circumstances. *Example:* "because someone flipped the switch" can explain a lamp being on; "because it is night" cannot. On the reading that the north wind and the day of the week are circumstances of the vane and the sign, nothing explains why the vane points north, and your two-part sign explanation is not one; on the reading that they are changes made to them, nothing changes. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained", and S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."
64	
65	**C6.** *In one sentence:* something whose answer is simply written into one of its parts is not an explanation at all. *Example:* a table that just lists the answers stops being an explanation. Your red-part and blue-part sign stays one on the reading that a part is "written in" only if it alone gives the answer everywhere asked; on the readings where giving it somewhere is enough, it stops being one. *Seems to go against* S45: "Yes, take the test out"; and, on those readings, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."
66	
67	**C7.** *In one sentence:* a link counts as found by trial even when nothing at all was tried, as long as nothing earlier already stood for the answer. *Example:* someone who has never seen a pendulum writes a formula on a napkin and says "this stands for the pendulum"; it counts as an explanation. A student copying it from a textbook still does not. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".
68	
69	**C8.** *In one sentence:* a worked-out link counts as worked out only if the explanation it leaned on while being worked out itself passes the tests. *Example:* a navigator works out a course with a method that fails on the open sea; her course still comes out right for the harbour, but on this reading it counts as merely declared. (Only on the reading that "worked out" asks about the explanation the working used.) On the same reading, an explanation of your weathervane worked out with a claim about another part of the vane that does not pass the tests stops being an explanation. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared" (her link was worked out), and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".
70	
71	**C11.** *In one sentence:* something whose answer is simply written into one part can pass the tests but is not an explanation. *Example:* "it is red because it is red" passes but does not count. Your two-part sign stays an explanation on the reading that a part is "written in" only if it alone gives the answer everywhere asked, and stops being one on the other readings. *Seems to go against* S45: "Yes, take the test out"; and, on those readings, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."
72	
73	**C12.** *In one sentence:* anything that passes the tests is an explanation, even if its link to the thing was only declared. *Example:* the student who copies a working pendulum formula and writes "this stands for the pendulum" has an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".
74	
75	**C15.** *In one sentence:* a question counts only if what it describes could be built in just one way; if several different set-ups would behave as described, nothing answers it. *Example:* "why is this lamp on at night and off at noon?" asked of any lamp that behaves so, when many different circuits do: on this reading no explanation of the lamp counts. On the reading where your sign is described only by what it shows (red on Mondays, blue on Tuesdays), several different signs would do that, so neither your two-part explanation nor any other explains it; the same for the weathervane. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation.", and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".
76	
77	**C16.** *In one sentence:* a link found by trying things counts as found only if the trying says what the link was built from; otherwise it counts as simply declared. *Example:* a gardener tries many watering schedules and keeps the one that works, but never writes down what it is made of; on this reading her schedule is merely declared, and explains nothing. An explanation of your sign or your weathervane reached by trying and keeping what worked, with nothing stated about how it was built, would stop being an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2, which set a link "simply declared" against one "found by trial or worked out"; and, for such a history, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation." and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".
78	
79	**C21.** *In one sentence:* a link counts as found by trial even when the answer was already written down in front of the person who picked it. *Example:* a student copies the pendulum formula from a textbook, checks it on one swing, and keeps it: on this reading that is an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".

## 4. For the owner: the flagged candidates in plain words

Each: one sentence, an everyday example, and the past decision it seems to go against, in the owner's words.

**C1.** *In one sentence:* each part of an explanation has to match what its piece of the thing does inside the whole, not the rule that piece follows on its own. *Example:* a bicycle's gear part may only say "the wheel turns at the speed it turns now with this rider", not "the gears multiply whatever the pedals do". On your shop sign, the red-part and blue-part explanation would no longer be an explanation, however the change of day is read. *Seems to go against* S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."

**C2.** *In one sentence:* only a question that was itself found or worked out can be answered; a question simply laid down has no answer. *Example:* a customer just asks "why is the sign red on Mondays?", with no story of how the question arose; on the reading that such a question counts as laid down, nothing explains the sign, the weathervane, or what your engineer's bridge creates. Where the question's story is recorded as found or worked out, nothing changes. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."; S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained"; S41 Q6: "Yes, it can".

**C5.** *In one sentence:* a difference counts towards an explanation only when it comes with a change made to the thing, not from its circumstances. *Example:* "because someone flipped the switch" can explain a lamp being on; "because it is night" cannot. On the reading that the north wind and the day of the week are circumstances of the vane and the sign, nothing explains why the vane points north, and your two-part sign explanation is not one; on the reading that they are changes made to them, nothing changes. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained", and S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."

**C6.** *In one sentence:* something whose answer is simply written into one of its parts is not an explanation at all. *Example:* a table that just lists the answers stops being an explanation. Your red-part and blue-part sign stays one on the reading that a part is "written in" only if it alone gives the answer everywhere asked; on the readings where giving it somewhere is enough, it stops being one. *Seems to go against* S45: "Yes, take the test out"; and, on those readings, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."

**C7.** *In one sentence:* a link counts as found by trial even when nothing at all was tried, as long as nothing earlier already stood for the answer. *Example:* someone who has never seen a pendulum writes a formula on a napkin and says "this stands for the pendulum"; it counts as an explanation. A student copying it from a textbook still does not. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".

**C8.** *In one sentence:* a worked-out link counts as worked out only if the explanation it leaned on while being worked out itself passes the tests. *Example:* a navigator works out a course with a method that fails on the open sea; her course still comes out right for the harbour, but on this reading it counts as merely declared. (Only on the reading that "worked out" asks about the explanation the working used.) On the same reading, an explanation of your weathervane worked out with a claim about another part of the vane that does not pass the tests stops being an explanation. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared" (her link was worked out), and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".

**C11.** *In one sentence:* something whose answer is simply written into one part can pass the tests but is not an explanation. *Example:* "it is red because it is red" passes but does not count. Your two-part sign stays an explanation on the reading that a part is "written in" only if it alone gives the answer everywhere asked, and stops being one on the other readings. *Seems to go against* S45: "Yes, take the test out"; and, on those readings, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."

**C12.** *In one sentence:* anything that passes the tests is an explanation, even if its link to the thing was only declared. *Example:* the student who copies a working pendulum formula and writes "this stands for the pendulum" has an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".

**C15.** *In one sentence:* a question counts only if what it describes could be built in just one way; if several different set-ups would behave as described, nothing answers it. *Example:* "why is this lamp on at night and off at noon?" asked of any lamp that behaves so, when many different circuits do: on this reading no explanation of the lamp counts. On the reading where your sign is described only by what it shows (red on Mondays, blue on Tuesdays), several different signs would do that, so neither your two-part explanation nor any other explains it; the same for the weathervane. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation.", and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".

**C16.** *In one sentence:* a link found by trying things counts as found only if the trying says what the link was built from; otherwise it counts as simply declared. *Example:* a gardener tries many watering schedules and keeps the one that works, but never writes down what it is made of; on this reading her schedule is merely declared, and explains nothing. An explanation of your sign or your weathervane reached by trying and keeping what worked, with nothing stated about how it was built, would stop being an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2, which set a link "simply declared" against one "found by trial or worked out"; and, for such a history, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation." and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".

**C21.** *In one sentence:* a link counts as found by trial even when the answer was already written down in front of the person who picked it. *Example:* a student copies the pendulum formula from a textbook, checks it on one swing, and keeps it: on this reading that is an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".

## 5. Gaps

- **The readings the owner's cases turn on remain the owner's**: the change as an edit or a boundary (C5; the mixed encoding is the computing agent's), D6.3's quantifier (C6, C11), a question's recorded history (C2), Desc's grain (C15). Each was computed under every choice named; which one the owner means is for the yes-or-no step.
- **Still computed one way only**: what V2.5 does to (Suff)'s defeat set (e2.14b); C16 and C21 on the owner's own cases were computed on the program's encodings with a selection history, not on a history the owner described; the bridge carries no candidate, so no candidate's effect on it as an explanation is computed (only its provenance and CreateEx, C2).
- **Not computed**: the ten variants flagged out of scope (§3); D5.7, whose one variant (R2V2.7) rewrites a FROZEN sentence and belongs to Part B.
- Whether gaps remain that bear on the explanation definition is the map's §7: on this list, none that a third round of Part A could reach inside its rule, pending the GLM cross-examination.

## 6. Unsure

- The decisions named are this agent's reading of the owner's words against the computed effect; each FLAG says only that the candidate does not appear to agree (S52). S41's questions are Claude's; only the owner's chosen answers are quoted as the owner's. Every quotation was compared with `records/Semantics - Decisions.md` (rule 14).
- C16's S41 Q2 flag reads the owner's question as contrasting "found by trial" with "simply declared"; C16 moves a found-by-trial link to declared, which is the opposite direction to C7, C12 and C21.
- The everyday examples are this agent's, written to show the sentence, not computed cases; the owner's own cases (the shop sign, the weathervane, the pendulum formula, the bridge) are the computed ones.
- Nothing here says what hard to vary covers (S33, S34), what must happen to candidates (S21), or which candidate to prefer (S20).

[Claude's reading: for non-scientific theories, candidate explanations attempt to solve a problem, and two may both appear to solve it; choosing one means that the chooser sees no option but the one not ruled out by its best argument, which is not to say the chooser has no option; if both survive, no resolution has been reached, further investigation is required and may solve the problem, and the problem may be ill posed; what happens to the candidates, and resolution, are up to the person choosing, and the owner claims nothing about what must happen: a problem judged low priority may be abandoned, and an interrupted episode may never resolve and may fade; choice is always important because no creative agent is infallible; creative agents are always constrained in some way, and the owner calls these all valid choices, whether or not their rationality is ever examined; a candidate needs to match the problem if resolution is the goal, but “matches the problem” is always tentative and may be wrong; in science it must match reality, but not by some fixed infallible metric; and creativity may or may not lead to a metric. It says "On the reading where your sign is described only by what it shows (red on Mondays, blue on Tuesdays), several different signs would do that, so neither your two-part explanation nor any other explains it". Good — two-part.

**C16** (R2V3.5): "a history that states no construction has an empty population of candidate transports, so nothing on it is selected". Admits: none. Drops: "every selected candidate whose history states no construction: every account on such a history (1,013 / 881 / 232 / 1,670 generated), the pole's forward candidate; the owner's sign and vane on a selection history; FC12.new2, FC30.new1, FC77, FC102.new1, FC104.new1 move". Section 3 §3 R2V3.5: "every account on a Sel history out (1,013 / 881 / 232 / 1,670)"; §9 suite moves FC12.new2, FC30.new1, FC77, FC102.new1, FC104.new1 (status). §10: "out 30: every candidate meeting (E) on the 'Sel' history ... all 8: the vane and both signs, in every encoding". Matches. The list says "the pole's forward candidate" — §3: "the pole's forward candidate on the 'Sel' history: Sel T → F, Dec F → T". Yes.

Flags: "**S41 Q2**: the owner's question set a link 'simply declared' against one 'found by trial or worked out'; here a link found by trial counts as declared unless its construction is stated. **S44** and **S41 Q15** on a selection history only". Hmm — S41 Q2's flag here is not marked "on that reading" — but the S44/Q15 flags are "on a selection history only". Is a selection history a reading of the owner's case? The owner's cases (sign, vane) — do they have selection histories? The histories are hand-set (I90). The owner never described the history of how the sign explanation was reached. So "on a selection history" is a condition, not really a "reading of the owner's own case" in the same sense as edit/boundary. Hmm. The §5 Gaps says "C16 and C21 on the owner's own cases were computed on the program's encodings with a selection history, not on a history the owner described". OK, that's named as a gap. Fine.

But wait — the S41 Q2 flag for C16: is that a decision the computation reaches? C16 moves found-by-trial links to declared. The owner's Q2 answer: "No, not if just declared" — about a student copying a formula with the link "simply declared, not found by trial or worked out". C16 makes found-by-trial count as declared when no construction is stated — which makes MORE things declared, hence fewer explanations. The owner's Q2 says declared links are not explanations; C16 makes some found-by-trial links declared, so they stop being explanations. Does that "not appear to agree with" S41 Q2? The list's §6 Unsure says: "C16's S41 Q2 flag reads the owner's question as contrasting 'found by trial' with 'simply declared'; C16 moves a found-by-trial link to declared, which is the opposite direction to C7, C12 and C21." So the flag rests on reading the owner's question as setting up a contrast — which is a reading of the owner's words, not of a case. Is that "a reading the owner's own cases turn on"? Not exactly; it's a reading of the owner's decision itself. Hmm. The list flags it without "on that reading" but flags the reading in §6 Unsure. Section 3 §3 says "Flag: S41 Q2 in reverse (the reply: 'it declares more, which Q2 permits'); see the candidate list" — note: the reply says Q2 PERMITS declaring more. So the computing agent's reply thought C16 does NOT depart from Q2. The list flags it anyway, with the unsure note. Is flagging it right or wrong? S52: "you flag discovered candidates that don't appear to fit decisions I've made in the past". The bar is "don't appear to fit". C16 arguably appears not to fit S41 Q2 on the reading that "found by trial" excludes "declared". Flagging with the unsure note seems defensible. And the settling agent will decide. I won't object strongly, though I could note the direction issue — it's already noted in §6. OK.

**C17** (R2V3.2): "a provenance record keyed by the change of contract (the program's reading), not by the new contract (the formal core's words)". Drops: "against the core's words: every account on a history that re-enters a contract whose record is not of that change (the reply's q = [C′, C, C]): 1,013 / 881 / 232 / 1,670 on re-entry histories; 58,880 held chain outputs (n ≤ 4)". Section 3 §3 R2V3.2: "the core and the program part on re-entry chains (2,147,344 chains n ≤ 4, cut T′: Dec F → T on 14,592 + 44,288 held outputs, 'contract' → 'change')". 14,592 + 44,288 = 58,880. Matches. none found (the bridge keeps one contract). OK.

**C18** (R2V3.3 (b)): "a construction trace is the whole subhistory from its start to the output, the record clause kept". Drops: "every held output whose trace spans an unrecorded change of contract: 45,072 of 341,184 chains (n ≤ 4, cut T′)". Section 3 §3 R2V3.3(b): "Dec F → T on 45,072 held outputs (341,184 chains n ≤ 4, cut T′)". Matches. none found. OK.

Wait — C18's statement: "a construction trace is the whole subhistory from its start to the output, the record clause kept" — and its drops: "every held output whose trace spans an unrecorded change of contract: 45,072". With the variant ON, these become... admitted (Dec F → T means they become explanations). "Drops" column showing 45,072 — hold on. Under R2V3.3(b), Dec F → T on 45,072 held outputs — that means these candidates become NOT declared, i.e., they become explanations (admitted), not dropped! Let me re-read. Section 3 §3 R2V3.3 (b): "(b) the trace spanning o1…o_t across an unrecorded change: Dec F → T on 45,072 held outputs". Hmm, Dec F → T: Dec was F and becomes T. Dec(t) means "the link is declared". ¬Dec(t) is required for being an explanation. So Dec F → T means they BECOME declared → they STOP being explanations → they DROP. Wait, I need to check what Dec means. In C9: "C9 admits every account on a history with an unrecorded change... 1,013..." — C9 (V3.5) is "an episode needs no provenance record of a change of contract", which admits candidates on unrecorded-change histories. And section 3's §3 for R2V3.2: "key 'contract' (the core's words): Episode T, Dec F" vs "key 'change': Episode F, ... Dec T". Hmm confusing.

Let me think: Dec(t) = the link t is merely declared (not found by trial or worked out). Being an explanation requires Account ∧ ¬Dec(t). So Dec T = declared (bad); Dec F = not declared (good).

R2V3.3(b): "Dec F → T on 45,072 held outputs" — Dec goes from F to T, i.e., these outputs become declared → stop being explanations → DROP. Wait but that contradicts what I said about the record clause. R2V3.3(b) is "the trace's extent = the whole subhistory... the record clause kept". With the trace spanning an unrecorded change of contract, the record clause bites: the construction is invalid (a change of contract mid-trace without a record), so the worked-out link counts as declared → Dec T. So yes, 45,072 DROP. And section 3's summary row: "Discovered changes to which count as explanations with (E) unchanged: ... R2V3.3 (b) (spanning traces)". "Changes to which count as explanations" — ambiguous, but drop is a change. OK so C18's drops = 45,072 held outputs. And C18's admits = none ("–"). Hmm wait, but §3 says "reproduces the second checker's e3.25c (45,072) with the clause kept". And C9 row: C9 admits... on spanning chains. C9 with spanning extent: "'C9′' (C9 read with the whole-subhistory extent) = C9 on spanning traces" — hmm. C9 is V3.5 "an episode needs no provenance record of a change of contract" — deleting the record clause. C18 is keeping the record clause but extending the trace. These interact. Anyway, the list's numbers match section 3. Fine.

Actually wait — I should double check the direction: section 3 §3 R2V3.3 row says "(b) the trace spanning o1…o_t across an unrecorded change: Dec F → T on 45,072 held outputs (341,184 chains n ≤ 4, cut T′)". And the list C18 drops: "every held output whose trace spans an unrecorded change of contract: 45,072 of 341,184 chains". Match. Good.

**C19** (R2V3.4): "a transport's parts are its ports (or its edits) with their bindings". Admits: "a transport with an extra part a stated construction lacks: 'Sel-parts' 356 (ports) / 1,013 (edits), t′ with an idle part 1,013 (SMALL); newly underdetermined pairs +1,041 / +1,141". Section 3 §3 R2V3.4: "ports and edits: t′ in 𝒯, Dec F, an explanation; t on 'Sel-parts' (stated lacks c_L): Dec T under ports, F under edits. Generated (ports / edits): 'Sel-parts' in 356 / 1,013 (SMALL), t′ idle in 1,013 / 1,013, t′ deviating in 576 / 638, newly underdetermined pairs 1,041 / 1,141". Matches. Drops: none. none found. OK.

**C20** (R2V3.7): "'earlier or the same' is one step back or the same, not any number of steps". Drops: "a construction whose witness lies two or more steps before its output: every account on such a tag history (1,013 / 881 / 232 / 1,670); CT8's R1, R3 (constructed → declared); chains: 4,224 + 11,520 held outputs Dec F → T; CreateEx on 3 of 1,024 valuations". Section 3 §3 R2V3.7: "generated: every account on the 'Con-far' tag history out (1,013 / 881 / 232 / 1,670); chains n ≤ 4, cut T′: Dec F → T on 4,224 (trace at o_t, output not held) and 11,520 (trace spanning); CT8's R1, R3: constructed → declared; (EX): CreateEx T → F on 3 of 1,024 valuations". Matches. Rests on: "the tag encoding (I56)". none found. OK.

**C21** (R2V2.6, at the reply's reach): "a selection counts even where the answer was already represented earlier in the history". Admits: "the student's copy of the pendulum formula (FC30.new1 (d)); CT8's R2, R4". Drops: none. Section 2: R2V2.6 at the reply's reach (whole exclusion dropped): "the student's copy Sel, FC30.new1 (d) and 4 more claims move, CT8's R2, R4 selected". Matches. Rests on: "the reply's reading of D11.2's deletion (P-R2S2-2)". Flag: S41 Q2 ("No, not if just declared") — FLAGGED (on the reply's reading). Good — marked "on the reply's reading", leaving the reading open. OK.

Now check §3 "Not in the list": R2V3.8 against S41 Q23 ("Yes, it's an argument") and R2V4.7 against S28. These are recorded but not flagged as candidates. The brief says "Is every decision it does not appear to agree with named" — these aren't candidates so not in scope of the flags; they're "recorded for the orchestrator". Hmm, but S52's yes-or-no step is about candidates. R2V3.8/R2V4.7 don't change which candidates are explanations, so they're not candidates; recording their tension with decisions for the orchestrator seems right. But wait — should they be flagged to the owner? S52: "Then you flag discovered candidates that don't appear to fit decisions I've made in the past". Only candidates. R2V3.8 and R2V4.7 are not candidates (they change arguments/ruling out, not explanation). So not flagged for the owner's yes-or-no — correct. Good.

Now the corrections O1–O4 from round 1's review. Let me read the round-1 files to verify the list carries them: C4's row mentions O3 (FC46's accounts 962 → 927...), C5's row mentions O4 (a second reading through τ, V2.3b: 6 more accounts drop), C7's row mentions O2 (e2.14b never computed). 49	| S3 | Sonnet | "FC107 under V2.4 differs only in a printed generated label". Its own printout shows Acc True → False for the identity candidate on p_δ, which is the r11 (Bearing) edge |
50	| S4 | Sonnet | "(Suff)'s defeat set and Out_j are not program functions". 51	| S5 | Sonnet | Its problem proxy puts Acc in place of NotOut_j (D10.1). The added edge "V2.1 adds kind-ii problems (47 → 57)" and the V2.3 and V2.4 problem counts rest on that proxy, not on D10.1 |
52	| S6 | Sonnet | r5 and r7 are marked computed (see the edge table) |
53	| S7 | Sonnet | Unbacked generalisations. First: "the candidate with no commitments meets (E) whenever the answer varies over C" rests on one case, and 0 of the 355 generated worlds with no commitments moved. Second: it marks the reply's "newly meeting (E): the written-in candidate" as contradicted by reading it as L273, but the reply names a class of candidates |
54	| O1 | Opus | It left out the hypothesis counts as "timed", so it missed that FC50 (a) becomes vacuous under V2.6, and the count moves |
55	| O2 | Opus | It marks R12, R15 and R17 computed although a part of each is unsettled, which its own row text says. Its "14 computed" overstates |
56	| O3 | Opus | N16 says "no claim builds a candidate whose Dependence needs a block of two or more (FC37–FC40 test set systems)". But under V2.2, FC46's accounts drop from 962 to 927, and the FC29, FC37 and FC51 counts move. The gap it names (no claim's *result* separates V2.2) still holds |
57	| O4 | Opus | It did not examine the reading of V2.3 through τ, which Sonnet's V2.3b shows matters (6 accounts) |
58	
59	**Time.** Sonnet 5.5 took 76 min 25 s (timing.txt: 21:32:25–22:48:50; commit a374058 at 22:48:58). Opus 5.5 took about 61 min, from its copy (18:37) to its commit 6e17160 (19:38:23), while three other section agents ran (load 5–8 on 4 cores).
60	
61	## 2. Verdict
62	
63	On what can be counted, Sonnet 5.5 matched Opus 5.5:
64	- the same variants and the same code for five of them;
65	- the same moves on the worked cases;
66	- generated-world counts of the same size, reproducible on rerun;
67	- the same suite results for five of seven variants;
68	- 12 of 20 edge statuses the same.
69	
70	It did three things better:
71	- it reported the count moves (FC50 (a) vacuous under V2.6);
72	- it built a finite analogue of L311;
73	- it tested V2.3's reading through τ.
74	
75	Its "mixed" labels are more careful than Opus's "computed".
76	
77	It fell short where the job is analysis rather than bookkeeping:
78	- two variants reached only part of the program, so their suite results and one edge the reply got wrong (V2.4's quantifier) were missed;
79	- the reply's V2.5 claim was accepted on a history set by hand, where the program's own history for the copy says otherwise;
80	- it misread one line of its own output (FC107);
81	- it said functions were missing that exist;
82	- a proxy misread a definition (D10.1);
83	- two edges were marked computed where a closer reading, or a search for a counterexample, contradicts them.
84	
85	Every one of these needed an Opus check to find. It also took longer than Opus did under heavier load.
86	
87	It genuinely helps as an **independent second computation**: agreement on the numbers is worth having, and it found one thing Opus missed. It does not genuinely help as **the agent of record** for this kind of analysis. Its errors are the quiet kind, a variant that reaches part of the program or a claim read too loosely, and they pass without a reviewer. On this trial the answer to S46 ("maybe analysis isn't something it should be used for. Unless it's something that genuinely helps") is:
88	- yes for a replication that Opus reviews;
89	- no as a replacement for the Opus computation or its review.
90	
91	Sonnet's mechanical jobs stay as S46 has them.
92	
93	Reviewed by one Opus 5.5 agent, 28 September 2026. Reruns: FC23.new1 and FC107 under V2.4, FC30.new1 under V2.5, in both copies; Opus's `s108_s2_routes.py` (identical to its printout); Sonnet's `s108_section2_worlds.py` V2.2 and V2.4 (identical to its printouts).

- the same variants and the same code for five of them;
- the same moves on the worked cases;
- generated-world counts of the same size, reproducible on rerun;
- the same suite results for five of seven variants;
- 12 of 20 edge statuses the same.

- it reported the count moves (FC50 (a) vacuous under V2.6);
- it built a finite analogue of L311;
- it tested V2.3's reading through τ.

Its "mixed" labels are more careful than Opus's "computed".

It fell short where the job is analysis rather than bookkeeping:
- two variants reached only part of the program, so their suite results and one edge the reply got wrong (V2.4's quantifier) were missed;
- the reply's V2.5 claim was accepted on a history set by hand, where the program's own history for the copy says otherwise;
- it misread one line of its own output (FC107);
- it said functions were missing that exist;
- a proxy misread a definition (D10.1);
- two edges were marked computed where a closer reading, or a search for a counterexample, contradicts them.

Every one of these needed an Opus check to find. It also took longer than Opus did under heavier load.

It genuinely helps as an **independent second computation**: agreement on the numbers is worth having, and it found one thing Opus missed. It does not genuinely help as **the agent of record** for this kind of analysis. Its errors are the quiet kind, a variant that reaches part of the program or a claim read too loosely, and they pass without a reviewer. On this trial the answer to S46 ("maybe analysis isn't something it should be used for. Unless it's something that genuinely helps") is:
- yes for a replication that Opus reviews;
- no as a replacement for the Opus computation or its review.

Sonnet's mechanical jobs stay as S46 has them.

Also harness jobs: md5 checks (`md5_check.py`), the key grep before each commit (`key_grep.py`), watching the run (`watch_run.py`). Any failure, any mismatch, any difference from what the computing agent expects goes to the computing agent (Opus), which says the cause and decides. A computing agent may not run the whole suite itself in place of the harness; where the harness cannot start, it runs the same script and records the departure (lesson S19). Sonnet in the harness never judges a variant, writes maths or code for the program, or reviews.
- At most five Claude agents at a time, Sonnet agents included (S17).

## How the replies will be read

1. **Nothing is opened until all four calls end.** No reply, receipt, reasoning file, attempt file, stream file or guard log of round 2 is opened until every job has ended its last allowed pass: the run log holds `s108r2_glm_loop: every pass ended; …` and `loop ended <UTC time>`, and the process in the pid file has exited. The progress lines may be watched; they hold no reply text. If a call is still running 24 hours after the launch, the orchestrator may stop the runner by its PID and record the calls not ended as not returned.
2. **What counts as a reply.** As in round 1's rule 2: only `<tag>.response.txt`; failed calls count neither way; connection failures are not answers; a job failed on answers after pass 3 is final; a key in the output or a sandbox not unchanged is reported to the orchestrator before anything else is read.
3. **A reply is a set of variants and claims about them, not a result.** A trace is the reply's claim until computed; a "not run" case is run; an edge is a claim until the computation settles it; a settlement a reply proposes for a round-1 edge is a proposal until computed. It flags a variant that changes a FROZEN item or another section's item (recorded, not implemented), one that repeats a round-1 variant (recorded, not implemented again), one that adds prose (S40), and one that would move where values are placed. It lists, per section, the parts of the share no variant answers. It writes `results/S108 Part A round 2 - tabulation of the replies, before any ruling.md`, created at once and filled as it goes (lesson S28), and rules on nothing.
5. **Implementation and computation**, by Opus 5.5 agents (or as recorded under "Who does what"), at most one per section, each in its own copy of the program: a copy of round 1's copy of its section (`results/S108 Part A - computation/section <n> model/`), so that round 1's switchable readings stay available, copied into `results/S108 Part A round 2 - computation/section <n> model/`, round 1's copy never written. Each implements every in-scope variant as a reading the program can switch on and off (the current definition the default) and **computes** its actual effect on the explanation definition, Acc and Account ∧ ¬Dec(t), off and on, over the worked cases (with the owner's cases: the weathervane, the shop sign with one part and with two, the student's declared formula, the bridge), the external examples FC-E1 to FC-E5, the creative transport case CT1 to CT8, and the generated worlds at scale 4 (the candidates whose result differs, how many of each kind, and the smallest witness of each), as round 1's rule 5 says; the whole suite with the variant on is a harness job (above). In addition:
   1. **for a variant of a reading**, every round-1 candidate that rests on it (C1 to C13) is computed under each choice of the reading the variant names: what it admits and drops, and whether each of its flags stands, comes or goes;
   2. **for a claimed-only edge of round 1**, the settlement the reply proposes, or the nearest the program can compute, is computed, and the edge marked computed, contradicted, or not settled by computation (with what would settle it);
   3. **for V1.6's formula** (section 2), a description Desc (I76) is stated for each worked case it is computed on, as the computing agent's invention with the other choices.
   Where a variant cannot be implemented as written, the agent says why and implements the nearest reading it can state, recorded as its own invention (S36). Each writes `results/S108 Part A round 2 - section <n> - variants computed.md`, with its runs and a `.json` of its edges, created at once and filled as it goes. Nothing it writes is a change to the theory.
6. **The dependency map after round 2, by one Opus 5.5 agent**: `results/S108 Part A round 2 - the dependency map, after round 2.md` and `.json`, built on round 1's corrected map (`.md` 1da37cf057ff02047fdeb1ca740eb5d8, `.json` 7ce9b1c65b55487d79f0c1a427adc2d9), which is never written: every round-1 node and edge kept with its standing unless a round-2 computation changes it (each change recorded with the round-1 standing and what changed it); the new edges of round 2, each with what shows it and its standing (computed, contradicted, claimed only); and the gaps after round 2 (items still untouched, edges still unsettled, readings still computed one way only).
7. **The candidate list after round 2**, by the same agent: `results/S108 Part A round 2 - candidate definitions of explanation, after round 2.md`: round 1's C1 to C13, each with what round 2 computed of the readings it rests on (what it admits and drops, and its flags, under each choice), and the new candidates of round 2 (C14 on), each with its statement, what it admits and drops (computed), and the owner's decisions it does not appear to agree with, named, for the later step in which the owner answers yes or no (S52: "candidates that don't appear to fit decisions I've made in the past"). Nothing in the list is applied.
8. **One critical review, by a fresh Opus 5.5 agent** (S42, S52) that built nothing of Part A: reads the tabulation, the computations, the map and the list after round 2 against this rule, round 1's rule and the owner's words, reruns the program where it doubts a result, and writes `results/S108 Part A round 2 - critical review.md`. Where some computing was given to Sonnet 5.5, it also reads the Opus check. Nothing is final before it.
9. **The orchestrator decides contested points** (S13), with its reasons; it keeps the finding, or sends the contested points, all together, to at most one fresh Opus 5.5 second checker. Either way it is recorded.
10. **A third round of Part A only if gaps remain** after round 2 (items still untouched that bear on the explanation definition, or edges the computation could not settle), under its own rule, written and committed before sending. Otherwise Part A ends, and Part B follows (S52).
11. **Nothing in the theory's text or maths is changed by Part A.** Round 2 is an experiment on copies. Its outputs are the map and the list after round 2. The text, the formal core, the claims and the program after round 4, round 1's files and round 1's program copies are never written; nothing is written into `authority/`.
12. **Arguments, not numbers.** Four replies saying the same thing decides nothing; neither do the length or the confidence of a reply.
13. **The owner's words bind every finding as content**, as round 1's rule 13 lists them (S20, S21, S23, S25 to S28, S33, S34, S36, S40, S41 with S47, S43, S44, S45). A variant that explores what one of them would reject is computed like any other, and its entry in the list names the decision. The readings the owner's cases turn on (edit or boundary; D6.3's quantifier) are the owner's to settle: the list says only "on that reading".
14. **Quotations are compared** with the text or the maths; where a quotation is not found, that is recorded and the point is read on what the text says.
15. **Records, by Opus, and a plain-words file** (S48): after the review and the orchestrator's decisions, one Opus agent writes the records, and then `plain words/108 Part A round 2 - what the variations found, in plain words.md` for the owner, which says "candidate" or "explanation", never "model", for what the theory judges (S43).

## How the run is launched

From the repository root, after this file's commit is pushed, one process, detached so that it outlives the agent that starts it, the key loaded only into its own environment from the session's key file and never printed (the other keys unset):

```

```

The process id of the session leader (the `bash -c` that `setsid` starts; round 1's launch recorded a wrapper's pid first and corrected it) goes in `<scratchpad>/s108r2_glm_run.pid`. The launching agent hands back once the log shows all four calls sent. A watcher outside that agent waits for the run to end (lesson S14).

- The shares were written from round 1's corrected map and the second checker's list of gaps; the gaps' order is the review's. A share cannot hold every untouched middle sentence of a section (S1 has 132, S4 112): the briefs point to the map's §6.4 and name the stretches that bear most on the explanation definition.
- Two claimed-only edges are the owner's yes or no (e2.09, S45; e3.37b, S47 with S41 Q6): the briefs ask only to note them; no computation settles them.
- Whether Sonnet 5.5 computes any of round 2 is the orchestrator's choice, recorded before any reply is opened; this file does not make it.
- The decoy tests were not rerun (see "Tools"); routes they did not try are not shown closed.

Decided by Claude under decisions S13, S17, S18, S39, S40, S42, S43, S46, S48, S52 and S53, and the orchestrator's decisions on round 1's critical review. 28 September 2026.
